one_line_contribution: That the harm of failure-derived agent memory is a property of how the item is written rather than of failure information per se: verbatim erroneous actions retrieved from other episodes induce a dose-dependent reproduction of the same error class during task execution, negation notes sit in between, and a positive rewrite of the corrected procedure retains the corrective value without the drag -- i.e. contextual drag extended from in-task context to cross-episode retrieved memory, with framing as the manipulated variable.
closest_prior_work: Two verified papers together cover most of the ground. (a) Contextual Drag, arXiv:2602.04288 (verified via s2cli/Semantic Scholar: 'the presence of failed attempts in the context biases subsequent generations toward structurally similar errors from the context'). It already establishes the mechanism, the structural-similarity metric, and the persistence under feedback/self-verification; the proposal's contribution reduces to a change of delivery channel (retrieved cross-episode item instead of in-task attempt) plus a framing factor. Scope extensions of a named published effect are the weakest kind of novelty at ICLR. (b) Honest Lying: Understanding Memory Confabulation in Reflexive Agents, arXiv:2605.29463 (verified via s2cli/Semantic Scholar; NOT cited by the proposal and NOT in its collision check). It is on ALFWorld, defines a Reflection Repetition Rate for the agent re-committing the stored error, shows that reflective memory reinforces rather than corrects failure, and -- critically -- its mitigation is precisely a rewrite of how the failure note is produced (replacing open-ended self-diagnosis with programmatic extraction of trajectory-level failure signals), reporting RRR 0.64 -> 0.10. That is the same benchmark, the same primary metric family (error repetition from a stored failure note), and the same shape of fix (change the note's construction, not the retrieval). It does not run the F1/F2/F3/F4 content-matched framing factorial and does not do a dose sweep, so it is not a full collision, but a reviewer who finds it will say the headline ('rewrite the failure note and the repetition goes away, on ALFWorld') is already demonstrated with a larger effect than this proposal is likely to measure. Also adjacent and verified: Experience Memory Graph, arXiv:2607.13884 (correction patterns from failed + expert trajectories -- the F3 form, already deployed as a method), Mistake Notebook Learning, arXiv:2512.11485 (distilled notes, not verbatim failures), and Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs, arXiv:2605.12978 (verified; same trajectories yield qualitatively different memories under different write schedules, with an episodic-only control competitive with consolidation -- the write-path-decides-value thesis in a different guise, also uncited).
strongest_objection: The framings are not content-matched in the way the central claim requires, so the predicted ordering has a trivial explanation. F3 (positive rewrite of the corrected procedure) contains the correct action sequence; F1 (verbatim failed excerpt with a FAILED label) does not. Token-matching and filler padding equalize length, not information: F3 tells the agent what to do, F1 tells it only what someone else did wrong. If the result is F1 worst / F3 best, the paper will have shown that procedural instructions beat error exemplars -- which is not a framing effect and is not new -- and the abstract's claim that 'the benefit of failure memory depends on framing rather than on the presence of failure information' will not follow. The only genuinely matched contrast is F2 vs F3 (the same rule stated as a prohibition or as a prescription), and that is exactly the comparison the proposal's own P2 flags as its falsifier. In ALFWorld's small, templated action space that difference is plausibly a few points and lands inside this program's stated 0.05-0.14 run-to-run noise band, at which point the submission is a null on its own decisive test with a large confounded ordering around it. A second, related problem: 'tasks where the error class is applicable' does the heavy lifting in P1 and P4 but is never given a deterministic definition, and applicability correlates with the task family that similarity retrieval selects on, so the primary metric is computed on a post-hoc subset. Finally the budget arithmetic does not close: 6 conditions x 500 tasks x 3 seeds is 9k episodes for one backbone, and the plan lists three backbones plus a dose sweep and eight ablations, so the stated 'about 12k episodes' understates the real cost by roughly a factor of three to four.
what_would_fix_it: Make F2 vs F3 the headline, not a cell in an ordering. (1) Pre-register the F2/F3 contrast as the confirmatory test, power it against the null replicate, and demote F1/F4 to descriptive context -- the honest claim is 'prohibition vs prescription at identical propositional content', not 'framing beats failure'. (2) Add the information-content control the design currently lacks: an F3-shaped positive procedure derived from a *success* trajectory of the same family (same corrected procedure, no failure provenance). If F3-from-failure equals F3-from-success, the failure content contributes nothing and the paper's real finding is that failure provenance is inert -- a cleaner and more interesting claim than the one proposed. (3) Add an error-class-tag-only item ('this family often fails by acting on a closed receptacle', no actions, no procedure) to bound how much of the effect survives when all erroneous content is removed, which is also the natural zero-dose point of the dose sweep. (4) Give a deterministic, pre-registered applicability rule per error class computed from the task specification before any rollout. (5) Cite and position against arXiv:2605.29463 and arXiv:2605.12978, and run at least one published failure-memory system (ExpeL avoid-style insights or Mistake Notebook Learning notes) in its native form as a condition, so F1-F4 are not four items the authors wrote themselves. (6) State the expected base rate of each error class under the no-memory condition from pilot data; a 1.5x multiplier on E1 loops may be unreachable by ceiling.
missing_baseline: A positive rewrite derived from a successful trajectory rather than from a failure (same corrected procedure, no failure provenance). Without it, F3's win cannot be attributed to 'rewriting the failure' as opposed to 'giving procedural guidance', and the paper cannot claim the failure content carries any value at all. Secondary omissions a reviewer will also demand: an error-class-tag-only item with zero erroneous content (the true zero dose), and at least one published failure-memory method (ExpeL insights or Mistake Notebook Learning notes) run natively rather than four author-written framings.
preprint_collision: No verified collision on the exact factorial, but the check has a real hole. Queries I ran, all on channel (a) the s2cli literature command (Semantic Scholar + HuggingFace; WebSearch is unavailable in this session, so channel (b) was never used): [1] 'framing of failure memory in context causes agents to reproduce the error negative examples negation vs positive rewrite' --recent -> 2607.10608, 2606.22844, 2605.29463, 2605.06527, 2604.17658, 2512.11485, 2502.17091 (WildFrame: LLMs show human-like framing effects and are more influenced by positive reframing -- prior evidence that the proposal's predicted direction is the expected one). [2] 'negative demonstrations in context cause LLM to imitate the errors negation instructions do not do X backfire' (no recency filter) -> 2605.13829 (Negation Neglect: training on documents negating false claims makes models believe them), 2605.03052, 2511.10881, 2401.17390 -- adjacent support for the negation-is-harmful half, none on agent memory. [3] 'ExpeL insights from failure avoid rules retrieved trajectories ALFWorld agent experience memory positive rewriting' --recent -> 2608.11772, 2607.10608, 2605.29463, 2605.11882, 2603.10600, 2509.25370. [4] 'how failure feedback should be written phrasing of self-reflection notes affects error repetition agents rewrite corrective instruction' --recent -> 2608.24794, 2608.02636, 2607.13091, 2605.29463. [5] 'dose response number of erroneous examples in prompt error repetition rate LLM agent trajectory imitation' -> failure-attribution work only (2607.12747, 2606.00765, 2607.12397); the dose axis appears genuinely unstudied. [6] 'retrieved failed trajectories from other episodes make agents repeat the same mistake priming imitation of errors memory bank' --recent -> 2607.13884, 2607.10608, 2608.00017, 2605.29463, 2605.27762. [7] 'prohibition versus prescription phrasing of guidance rules for LLM agents positive reframing improves compliance avoid rules harmful' --recent -> nothing relevant (empty for this purpose). ID verification (s2cli paper): 2602.04288 VERIFIED (Contextual Drag, S2, 4 citations, matches the proposal's description), 2512.11485 VERIFIED (Mistake Notebook Learning, ACL, as described), 2605.08563 VERIFIED (Why Retrying Fails, context contamination on retry), 2606.31270 VERIFIED (Learning from Failure for computer-use agents), 2607.13884 VERIFIED (Experience Memory Graph), 2605.24941 VERIFIED (Memory-Induced Tool-Drift, personality bias, correctly set aside). Every ID the novelty argument leans on is real and described accurately, which is better than most submissions and I credit it. The hole: the check missed 2605.29463 (Honest Lying), which is on the proposal's own benchmark, defines a repetition-rate metric for a stored failure re-committed by the agent, and fixes it by changing how the note is written -- the single closest published result -- and 2605.12978 (Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated), which is the write-path-decides-value thesis at consolidation level and appears on the proposal's own novelty card at sim 0.59, unaddressed. Two of the card's top-five entries (2605.12978, 2607.13884) are given only a passing clause or none. So: a thorough, honest, well-instrumented check that nonetheless failed to surface the nearest neighbour, and the novelty score reflects what I verified rather than the check's confident closing sentence.
